prompt: The page is `http://localhost:8080/page.html`. Match each address to what the browser makes of it.
hint: An origin is the scheme, the host and the port, compared as written.

pairs.right: same origin: only the path differs

right_distractors: same origin: both names reach one machine

prompt: What does the same-origin policy keep a script on one origin from doing with another origin?
hint: The request is not the part it protects.

choices.text: Reading the response to a request it caused
choices.why: Right. The request may well go out; the answer is what the browser keeps from the script.

choices.text: Showing one of its images inside the page, with ``
choices.why: Embedding is allowed. What the script cannot do is read the image's bytes.

choices.text: Sending it a request of any kind, even a GET
choices.why: Forms, images and scripts have gone to other origins since long before CORS, and a simple request still goes out unasked.

choices.text: Opening a link to it
choices.why: Following a link is navigation, and the new page simply belongs to the other origin.

prompt: An API is called only by phone apps and by other servers. A developer says the same-origin policy keeps strangers out of it. What is wrong with that?
hint: Who enforces the policy?

choices.text: The policy covers phone apps too, but only over HTTPS
choices.why: No program but a browser applies it, over HTTP or over HTTPS.

choices.text: Nothing: the server refuses an unknown origin
choices.why: secure.py answered an unknown origin with 200 and the book; and these clients send no `Origin` at all.

choices.text: It keeps strangers out only once CORS is turned off
choices.why: CORS relaxes the policy, and neither of them does anything to a client that is not a browser.

choices.text: Only browsers apply the policy
choices.why: Right. An app or a server reads whatever comes back. The policy protects the person at a browser, and these clients have no such person to protect.

prompt: Why does the lesson put `page.html` in `~/shelf/site` and start `python3 -m http.server` there, rather than in `~/shelf`?
hint: What does that server hand out?

choices.text: `http.server` will not start where there are Python files
choices.why: It starts anywhere, and that is exactly the danger.

choices.text: It serves every file under it, `shelf.db` included
choices.why: Right. Anybody who reached port 8080 would download the database, and later the private keys.

choices.text: Two directories are what make the page and the API two origins
choices.why: An origin is scheme, host and port; directories play no part, and the ports are what differ here.

choices.text: Port 8080 serves HTML files and refuses the rest
choices.why: A port knows nothing about file types; `http.server` sends whatever file is asked for.

prompt: `secure.py` runs in the VM with its defaults. On your computer, the browser opens `http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/books/1` and the connection is refused. Why?
hint: Which machine does the browser mean by that address?

choices.text: CORS refuses connections from origins off the list
choices.why: CORS refuses no connection at all; it decides what a page may read once an answer has arrived.

choices.text: A browser needs HTTPS to reach a virtual machine
choices.why: Plain HTTP reaches a VM as well as anything else; the address is the problem.

choices.text: `secure.py` takes connections from curl and not from browsers
choices.why: It cannot tell which program connects. It listens on an address, and that one is the VM's own loopback.

choices.text: There it means your computer, not the VM
choices.why: Right. Nothing listens on your computer's port 8000, and the VM's 127.0.0.1 is another machine's loopback. The server has to listen on the VM's network address.

prompt: To be reachable from the browser on your computer, `secure.py` is started with `--host ___`, the address that stands for every address the VM has.
hint: Four numbers, all the same.

prompt: curl sends `GET /v1/books/1` to `secure.py` with `Origin: http://127.0.0.1:8080`, an origin not on its list. What comes back?
hint: Compare the two transcripts header by header.

choices.text: 200 and the book, with no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`
choices.why: Right. Both answers carried the book, and nothing but that one header told them apart.

choices.text: 200 with an empty body, so a page would see nothing
choices.why: The body was the whole book in both transcripts. Withholding it is the browser's job.

choices.text: 403 Forbidden, with an error naming the origin
choices.why: The server refuses nothing because of `Origin`; it leaves one header out.

choices.text: No answer: the connection closes before the request is read
choices.why: The request was read and answered, and the log printed a 200 for the browser's version of it too.

prompt: Which of these requests from a page does the browser send without a preflight? Choose all that apply.
hint: Could an HTML form have sent it?

choices.text: A GET with no headers set by the script
choices.why: Right. It is the request "Read it" sent, and it went straight out.

choices.text: A PATCH with a JSON body
choices.why: PATCH is not a simple method, and `application/json` is not a simple type: two reasons to ask first.

choices.text: A POST of form fields, `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`
choices.why: Right. A form has always been able to send exactly this, so CORS adds no question in front of it.

choices.text: A GET carrying an `Authorization` header
choices.why: The method is simple but the header is not on the safelist, so the browser asks first.

choices.text: A POST whose body is `application/json`
choices.why: POST is a simple method, but this `Content-Type` is not one of the three a form can send.

prompt: An API offers `GET /v1/books/1/sell`, which takes one copy off the stock. A page on an origin that is not on the list calls it with `fetch`. What happens to the stock?
hint: Is a GET asked about first?

choices.text: Unchanged: the browser refuses to send it
choices.why: A plain GET is simple and goes out unasked, as the log showed for the blocked page.

choices.text: Unchanged: the preflight is refused first
choices.why: A GET with no special headers gets no preflight at all.

choices.text: One less, and the page reads the new number from the answer
choices.why: The request goes through, but the answer names no origin, so the page reads nothing of it.

choices.text: One less; only the answer is hidden from the page
choices.why: Right. That is why a GET must change nothing: any page on any origin can make a browser send one.

prompt: Put in order what happens when the page on the list presses "Set the stock to 11".
hint: The script calls once; the browser makes two requests.
items: The script calls `fetch` with PATCH and a JSON body
`secure.py` answers 204, naming the origin, the methods and the headers
The script reads the new stock
trap: The PATCH does not leave until the answer to the OPTIONS has arrived and allowed it.

prompt: Match each thing a preflight is about to the header in the answer that settles it.
hint: One header in the answer has no question to answer.

pairs.left: how long the answer may be remembered

prompt: A page sends `Authorization: Bearer …` with its PATCH. The preflight's answer names the right origin and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type`. What happens?
hint: The browser compares what it asked for with what was allowed.

choices.text: The PATCH is not sent, though curl with the same token works
choices.why: Right. The header the script set was not among the ones allowed, so the browser stops at the question.

choices.text: The PATCH goes out without the header and gets a 401
choices.why: A browser does not trim a request to make it fit; it refuses the whole request at the question.

choices.text: The PATCH succeeds: `Authorization` is safelisted
choices.why: It is not on the safelist, which is why it causes a preflight at all.

choices.text: The server answers the preflight 401, because it came with no token
choices.why: A preflight carries no credentials, and `secure.py` answers it 204. The refusal is the browser's.

prompt: The page loaded from `127.0.0.1:8080` pressed "Set the stock to 11". According to the server's log, how many requests did that click make reach the server?
hint: Look at the last line of the log.

prompt: A server allows an origin when it ends in `shelf.example`. Which of these origins also gets through?
hint: Read the test as a string comparison, letter by letter.

choices.text: `https://shelf.example.org`
choices.why: It ends in `.org`, so the test refuses it. The hole is at the other end of the name.

choices.text: `https://shelf.example:8443`
choices.why: The port is part of the origin string, so it no longer ends in `shelf.example`.

choices.text: `https://notshelf.example`
choices.why: Right. It ends in the right letters, and it is a domain anybody is free to register. A set of exact origins has no such hole.

choices.text: `http://localhost:8080`
choices.why: It does not end in `shelf.example`, so the test refuses it.

prompt: An API names its allowed origins correctly but sends `Vary: Origin` on no answer, and a shared cache sits in front of it. Page A, on the list, asks for a book; then page B, also on the list, asks for the same book. What does B get?
hint: What did the cache keep, headers included?

choices.text: Its own answer, because caches ignore CORS headers
choices.why: A cache stores the whole answer, headers included, and without `Vary` it thinks one copy fits every page.

choices.text: A refusal, because the cache hands B the answer that names A
choices.why: Right. B is refused for a reason it cannot see. `Vary: Origin` makes the cache keep one copy per origin.

choices.text: Its own answer: each page triggers its own preflight
choices.why: A plain GET has no preflight, and a cached answer is served without asking the server.

choices.text: A 500, since a cache cannot store answers with CORS headers
choices.why: Caches store such answers happily. That is the whole problem.

prompt: Which of these stop a stranger's program from changing the stock through `secure.py`'s PATCH? Choose all that apply.
hint: curl changed the stock while claiming an origin nobody trusts.

choices.text: A shorter list of allowed origins
choices.why: CORS tells a browser what to show a page; a program that is not a browser ignores it.

choices.text: A token, checked on every request
choices.why: Right. Authentication works whatever the client is, browser or not, which CORS does not.

choices.text: Refusing every request with no `Origin` header
choices.why: A program sends whatever `Origin` it likes, so the header proves nothing about who sent it.

choices.text: A check that the caller's role may change stock
choices.why: Right. That is authorisation, lesson 11, and the server makes it for every request.

prompt: Over plain HTTP, a request carries `Authorization: Basic YW5hOmNvcnJlY3QtaG9yc2U=`. What can somebody reading the bytes on the way learn from it?
hint: What did `base64 -d` need?

choices.text: The user name and the password
choices.why: Right. `base64 -d` needed nothing but the header, and printed `ana:correct-horse`.

choices.text: Nothing, without the key that base64 was encrypted with
choices.why: Base64 has no key; it is a way of writing bytes as text.

choices.text: The user name; the password inside is hashed
choices.why: Nothing in the header is hashed. Both halves came back from one decoding.

choices.text: How long the password is, and nothing more
choices.why: The whole password is in there, written in another alphabet.

prompt: Put in order the steps that gave `secure.py` a certificate curl accepts.
hint: The authority exists before it can sign anything.
items: Make the CA's key and its self-signed certificate
Make the server's key and a certificate signing request
Sign the request with the CA's key and `server.ext`
trap: The names have to be written before the signing, because the signature covers them.

prompt: A colleague's script fails with `curl: (60) SSL certificate problem`, and they add `-k` to make it pass. What did they give up?
hint: TLS does two jobs.

choices.text: Encryption: with `-k` the request travels as plain text
choices.why: `-k` leaves the encryption on and stops checking the certificate, which is worse because everything looks fine.

choices.text: Knowing who is at the other end
choices.why: Right. The connection is encrypted to whoever answered, and nothing now says who that is.

choices.text: Nothing that matters on their own company's network
choices.why: Every network has other machines on it, and nothing now tells them apart from the server.

choices.text: HSTS, which `-k` switches off for that host
choices.why: curl applies HSTS only with `--hsts`; `-k` is about verifying the certificate.

prompt: `secure.py` sends `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000`. For how many days does a browser keep to HTTPS for that host?
hint: There are 86400 seconds in a day.

prompt: Match each header `secure.py` sends to what it tells the browser.
hint: Each one forbids something.

pairs.right: keep no copy of this answer
say nothing about this address when leaving it
let no page put this in a frame

prompt: An API answers only in JSON. Why does it still send `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'`?
hint: Think of an answer that ends up somewhere it was not meant to be.

choices.text: Browsers refuse JSON from another origin without it
choices.why: Reading JSON from another origin is CORS's question; CSP plays no part in it.

choices.text: It stops other origins sending requests to the API
choices.why: A CSP limits what a document loads. Requests to the API are not its business, and not even CORS stops them.

choices.text: It encrypts the JSON so that only allowed pages read it
choices.why: A header encrypts nothing; TLS does that, for every byte.

choices.text: An answer ever shown as a page then loads and runs nothing
choices.why: Right. JSON needs nothing, so forbidding everything costs nothing, and it disarms the one case where an answer is rendered.

prompt: `secure.py`'s `Server` header says `shelf` and no version. What does that change?
hint: Is the version itself a flaw?

choices.text: It fixes the known flaws of the Python it runs on
choices.why: The software is the same software; only updating it fixes its flaws.

choices.text: It no longer tells every client which known flaws to try first
choices.why: Right. It removes an advertisement, not a vulnerability. Keeping the software up to date is the fix.

choices.text: It makes the server refuse clients that ask for its version
choices.why: Nobody asks; the header goes out on every answer, unasked.

choices.text: Nothing, since browsers alone read that header
choices.why: Every client receives it, and scanners read it before anything else.

prompt: Match each OWASP API risk to the defence this course built for it.
hint: The table in the section has a column of lessons.

pairs.right: checking the caller against each object, lesson 11
CORS, headers and TLS on every answer, lesson 13
a written contract of every endpoint, lesson 6

prompt: An ordinary account calls `DELETE /v1/admin/users/7`, and user 7 is deleted. Which risk is that?
hint: The function itself should have been refused.

choices.text: API2 Broken Authentication
choices.why: The account was who it said it was. What nobody checked is what it was allowed to do.

choices.text: API1 Broken Object Level Authorization
choices.why: API1 is an allowed function used on the wrong object. Here an ordinary account should never reach the function.

choices.text: API6 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
choices.why: API6 is a permitted flow used too much. Here one call was enough, to a function the account should not have reached.

choices.text: API5 Broken Function Level Authorization
choices.why: Right. Every administrative function has to check the role or scope, whoever is calling.

prompt: A client sends `PATCH /v1/users/me` with `{"role": "admin"}` and becomes an administrator. Which defence was missing?
hint: The object was the client's own. The field was not theirs to set.

choices.text: Write rules per field (API3)
choices.why: Right. Changing your own profile is allowed; changing that property of it is not, and the write has to refuse the field.

choices.text: A rate limit on PATCH requests (API4)
choices.why: One request was enough; volume had nothing to do with it.

choices.text: CORS on the users endpoint (API8)
choices.why: curl sends this with no browser involved, so CORS plays no part.

choices.text: Checking the signature on the token (API2)
choices.why: The client was exactly who it said it was. The problem is what it was allowed to write.

prompt: Why is a server fetching an address a client supplied more dangerous than the client fetching it itself?
hint: Where is each of them standing on the network?

choices.text: The server's download ties up a thread for longer
choices.why: That is API4's worry, and a timeout settles it. SSRF is about where the request can go.

choices.text: The client's browser applies CORS and the server does not
choices.why: True, and beside the point: the danger is the server's position on the network, not a header.

choices.text: It sits inside a network that the client cannot see
choices.why: Right. From there it reaches `127.0.0.1`, the database and `169.254.169.254`, with the server's position and the server's trust.

choices.text: A long address may overflow the server's parser
choices.why: Long input is a different and smaller problem. A short address can reach the database.

prompt: shelf has to download a cover from an address a client sends. Which checks belong in front of that download? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section lists four.

choices.text: Hosts from an allowlist alone, over `https`
choices.why: Right. A list of destinations, compared exactly, is the first check and the strongest.

choices.text: Redirects followed freely, since the first address was checked
choices.why: A redirect is a second address, and the client may have chosen it too. Each one is checked again.

choices.text: The name resolved, and any address that is not public refused
choices.why: Right. `is_global` said `False` for loopback, a private network and the metadata address.

choices.text: `169.254.169.254` let through, as it is not a private network
choices.why: It is link-local, where clouds keep their metadata, and `is_global` said `False` for it.

choices.text: A timeout and a limit on the size
choices.why: Right. A slow or enormous answer must not hold the API's threads.

prompt: A partner's API sends shelf a book whose `price_cents` is `"free"` instead of a number. What should shelf do?
hint: Treat it as you would a client's request.

choices.text: Store it as it came, since the partner signed a contract
choices.why: A contract does not stop a bug or a compromise. Whatever is stored enters with shelf's own authority.

choices.text: Refuse it, as it breaks the agreed schema
choices.why: Right. A partner's answer is input, and it is validated like input.

choices.text: Store the fields that parse and drop the price
choices.why: Half an answer stored is a record nobody can trust. Refuse it whole and say why.

choices.text: Ask again with TLS verification switched off
choices.why: The format is the problem, not the connection, and verification stays on whatever happens.

prompt: Which of these is a line you can check against a deployed API, from outside?
hint: One curl command should settle it.

choices.text: The API follows good security practice in every endpoint
choices.why: True or false, no request can show it. It is a hope, not a check.

choices.text: The team takes security seriously
choices.why: A statement about people; nothing about the API answers it.

choices.text: Unknown origins get no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`
choices.why: Right. One curl with an `Origin` header settles it, today and after every change.

choices.text: The code was reviewed by somebody experienced before launch
choices.why: Worth doing, and invisible from outside: the review leaves nothing in an answer.

prompt: The checklist is gone through again after every ___ to the API, because a header lost in a refactor fails no test and breaks no page.
hint: Not once before launch.

prompt: A page served from `https://localhost:8080` calls `secure.py`, whose list of origins is still the default. The browser refuses to show it any answer. Why?
hint: Write out the page's origin and the one on the list.

choices.text: HSTS forbids cross-origin requests
choices.why: HSTS only decides that a host is reached over HTTPS; it says nothing about origins.

choices.text: The certificate does not cover port 8080
choices.why: Certificates name hosts, not ports, and the refusal here is CORS, not TLS.

choices.text: `https` is not `http`; the origin is off the list
choices.why: Right. The scheme is part of the origin, and the list holds `http://localhost:8080` only.

choices.text: A page served over HTTPS may not call any server at all
choices.why: It may; browsers stop an HTTPS page calling plain HTTP, but that is a different rule, and it is not what refuses here.

prompt: A signed-in page reads a user's orders from an API, with cookies (`credentials: "include"`). Which headers in the API's answer make that work without opening it to other sites? Choose all that apply.
hint: Credentials change what the browser accepts.

choices.text: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`
choices.why: Browsers refuse `*` on a credentialed answer; it would let every site read every user's orders.

choices.text: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` naming the page's exact origin
choices.why: Right. One origin, from a list, compared whole.

choices.text: `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`
choices.why: Right. Without it the browser keeps a credentialed answer from the page.

choices.text: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` copied from the request's `Origin`
choices.why: That names every origin that asks, which is `*` without the browser's safeguard.

choices.text: `Vary: Origin`
choices.why: Right. The answer depends on `Origin`, and a cache has to know it.

prompt: While testing, a developer opens `page.html` straight from disk, a `file://` address, and gets a CORS error. They add `null` to the allowed origins and it works. What else did they allow?
hint: Who else sends `Origin: null`?

choices.text: Every origin, because `null` works as a wildcard
choices.why: `*` is the wildcard. `null` is a value a few kinds of page send.

choices.text: Pages opened from her own disk, and nothing more
choices.why: `Origin: null` says nothing about where the page came from, and several kinds of page send it.

choices.text: Any sandboxed `iframe` that anybody puts on any site
choices.why: Right. A sandboxed frame sends `Origin: null` too, and anybody can publish one.

choices.text: Requests from curl, which sends `null` by default
choices.why: curl sends no `Origin` unless told to, and pays no attention to CORS in any case.
